title: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Repetitive patterns are common and some nested patterns are seen, but the more complicated kinds of patterns discussed in this chapter do not ever appear to have been used.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 2, “The Crucial Experiment”; section “Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before” (from p. 42), p. 43. Scope: historical ornamental art across cultures

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch02-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large open image collections can find counterexamples and estimate usage in covered collections. Their preservation and selection biases cannot confirm that such patterns never appeared across all historical ornament.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Search a temporally and culturally stratified corpus of ornament images using preregistered similarity features for repetitive, nested, and rule-30-like patterns, followed by expert validation. Any authenticated historical rule-30-like ornament refutes the absolute absence claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Digitized museum collections are not exhaustive across cultures.

Absence cannot be established from incomplete preservation.

Similarity to complex cellular-automaton output requires a threshold.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open museum collections and digitized pattern books are large enough for a systematic image search, and a single convincing match would refute the claim that such patterns were never used. They are a biased fraction of historical ornament, and the pattern classes need an explicit encoder. The universal historical negative is therefore only partly testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Encode repetitive, nested, and rule-30-like classes as image statistics and search digitized historical ornament for each class. A clear rule-30-like ornamental pattern refutes the universal absence. Finding none in the digitized corpus supports the claim only inside that corpus.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Stylized script and geometric craft can be misread as cellular-automaton patterns, and the reverse.

Survival and digitization favor some cultures and media, so absence in the corpus is not absence in history.
